title: Installing an airtight membrane on walls and ceilings
subtitle: Achieving a continuous air barrier during internal wall insulation or loft conversion work
excerpt: An airtight membrane creates a continuous air barrier across walls and ceilings to prevent warm moist air from moving into the insulation layer and condensing. It is the critical element in a low-energy retrofit and requires careful lapping, taping, and sealing at every junction.
sourceNotes: AECB (Association for Environment Conscious Building) guidance on airtightness membranes and taping. BRE Digest 369 on condensation in buildings. Passive House Institute technical guidance on air barrier continuity. Building Regs Approved Document F on ventilation strategy after air-tightening.

glossaryTerms.definition: A membrane placed on the warm side of insulation to limit water vapour diffusion into the insulation layer.
A membrane that forms a continuous air barrier across the building envelope, distinct from but often combined with a vapour control layer.
A path through a building element that conducts heat more readily than the surrounding insulation, creating a cold spot.

content.text: An
airtightness membrane

is a sheet of polythene or specialist membrane fixed continuously across the warm face of the insulation layer. Its job is to stop warm moist air from the room from moving into the insulation, where it would cool and condense. The membrane is not a
vapour control layer
(which limits vapour diffusion). An airtightness membrane stops convective air movement, which is a faster and more damaging route for moisture transfer.

In practice, most modern membranes do both jobs. A 1,500-gauge polythene sheet stops air movement but degrades over decades. A specialist Pro Clima or similar product is designed for the lifetime of the building and includes integrated tape adhesive zones at edges.
What you need to know first
The membrane only works if it is continuous. A single 20 mm gap around a socket or pipe penetration can negate 90% of the benefit. Plan every penetration before you start.

After fitting an airtight membrane and drylining over it, the room is more airtight than before. Check that the room has adequate ventilation: a trickle vent in a window, or a background ventilator, is the minimum for a habitable room.
Membrane on the ceiling must lap down to meet the wall membrane by at least 150 mm, with that overlap taped. The junction between ceiling and wall is the most common continuity break.
Installing the membrane: walls
Fix the insulation layer to the wall (PIR board on dabs, or between timber studs). Leave the surface smooth and level; membrane bridging a lump of adhesive will develop a stress point.
Roll the membrane horizontally starting from the ceiling junction. Staple into the top plate or ceiling batten at 150 mm intervals. Pull the membrane tight but not taut.
Lap each horizontal row over the one below by at least 150 mm. Tape the overlap using a compatible membrane tape. Rub the tape firmly with a squeegee.
At corners, cut the membrane to fold around the corner rather than butting two sheets; a fold is inherently more continuous than a taped junction.
At every penetration (socket, pipe, cable), apply a proprietary collar or acoustic socket box that integrates with the membrane. Seal the collar to the membrane with tape on all four sides.
Installing the membrane: ceiling

Ceiling membranes are most commonly fitted during a loft conversion or when re-boarding a ceiling below a cold loft. Run the membrane across the full ceiling with 150 mm laps between sheets. The membrane must extend past the wall plate and down the inner face of the wall by at least 150 mm so it can lap with the wall membrane.
The
thermal bridge
at the wall-ceiling junction

The top of the dry-lined wall meets the ceiling. If the ceiling insulation stops at the wall plate and the wall insulation stops at the ceiling, there is a gap at the junction through which cold can bypass both layers. The membrane continuity lap addresses air movement. A small strip of 50 mm PIR board cut to fit the zone above the wall plate addresses the conductive bridge.
What done well looks like

The membrane is continuous with no unintentional holes. All laps are taped. All penetrations have collars. A smoke pencil test or incense stick held around sockets and pipe entries shows no airflow on a windy day. A blower door test conducted on the finished building shows a measurable improvement in the airtightness score.
Troubleshooter

rows.symptom: Condensation appears on the inner face of the membrane after fitting
rows.cause: The membrane is on the cold side of the insulation, not the warm side
rows.fix: Remove and refit. The membrane always goes between the insulation and the plasterboard, never between the wall and the insulation.

rows.symptom: Tape fails to stick to the membrane edge
rows.cause: Membrane surface is dusty or cold; or wrong tape used
rows.fix: Wipe the membrane surface with a dry cloth. Apply in temperatures above 10°C. Use only the membrane manufacturer's approved tape for that product.
